newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Electra NAV rises, but cautious on buyouts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Electra NAV rises, but cautious on buyouts.

text.p: British private equity specialist Electra Investment Trust (EIT) on Friday reported a 9.12 percent increase in its adjusted net asset value (NAV) per share, a faster increase than the 7.9 percent rise a year ago.
But EIT chairman Michael Stoddart cautioned that conditions in the private equity market were growing more difficult.
Funds have flowed into the sector in increasing amounts, he said, "and as a result prices are now reaching levels where it may be more difficult to achieve the rates of return which we require."
"We are unwilling to pay unrealistic prices and are therefore increasingly selective in making investments."
EIT's current pipeline of deals is strong, Stoddart said, and the trust is concentrating on sectors within private equity with less competition and on developing innovative structures.

"I am reasonably confident that we have a good basis and there are reasonable opportunities," Stoddart said, adding that he believes the trust remains well positioned to outperform the FTSE all-share index.
EIT set its interim dividend at 4.5 pence per share, a 15 percent increase over the same period last year, while also retaining 2.1 million stg for consolidated revenue reserves.
NAV at the end of the period was 569.74 pence per share.
Return on investments in unlisted companies got a big boost in the period from the sale of privatised rolling stock operating company Eversholt.

EIT invested 17 million stg in Eversholt in February 1996, realising a profit of 75 million stg when it was sold to HSBC Group a year later. About 58 million stg of the profit was booked in the period.
Analysts were mixed in their reactions to the results.
"Overall we were slightly disappointed," said Carolyn Coke, of NatWest Securities.
"A lot of the uplift came from one deal, Eversholt. If you strip that out they were only up 3 percent."

Coke said Electra told analysts at a meeting Friday that it had been less aggressive in valuing its private equity portfolio than it would have been if they had not booked such a big gain on Eversholt.
"There may be some hidden value there," she said.

"It was slightly lower than people were going for but they still had a very good half," said Philip Middleton of Merrill Lynch, adding that he is still very positive on the trust on a long-term outlook.
EIT was at 480 pence per share in late morning trading, down 1.5 pence from Thursday's close.
This represents a discount of about 16 percent from NAV.
Private equity portfolio sales in the half year generated 172 millions stg, Stoddart said, and brought net borrowings to virtually nothing.
Stoddart said private equity investment in the period was 111 million stg, down from 118 million in the same period last year.
High valuations in the buyout market in the U.S. and UK are causing the trust to look increasingly at alternative markets, Stoddart said, but he is cautious on continental Europe.
"For instance, labour problems in France are very difficult to control. On paper you may be buying at 75 percent of the PE that you are paying in the UK but there are inherent dangers."
Several major UK institutions, including Schroders and Charterhouse, have launched European private equity funds in recent weeks. adding more than 1.5 billion stg to the sector.
Management buy-outs of unprofitable companies are an area of increased interest for EIT, Stoddart said, as competition is less and the efforts of new management can boost returns.
For the 12 months ending March 1997, EIT's adjusted NAV per share increased by 20 percent, outpacing a 13.9 percent increase
